problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $L{u(t-4)\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\pi t)},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

activity_context.topic_title: The Second Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms

feedback.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $L{u(t-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t)},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
feedback.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}={e}^{-as}\,L{g(t+a)},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L{u(t-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t)}.
$$

Therefore, $a=1,$ and we have 

$$
L{u(t-1)\,g(t)}={e}^{-s}\,L{g(t+1)},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi (t+1)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t+3\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

and by the sum formula for cosine, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t+3\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡3\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡3\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡3\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+1)} & =L{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t)} \\  & =-L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi t)} \\  & =-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-1)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-s}\,L{g(t+1)} \\  & =-{e}^{-s}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+9{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
